items.text:
Your first month as a manager is not a test of how much you can personally carry.

One of the fastest ways to become the bottleneck is to delegate vaguely, get nervous, then take the work back.

A cleaner handoff has four parts:
• the outcome
• the constraints
• the checkpoint
• the finish line

When those are clear, you can manage without hovering — and your team can work without guessing.

Plain Act is built for these pressure moments in the first 30 days: authority, feedback, delegation, managing up, pushback, and decision timing.

The practical manual: https://plainact-crypto.github.io/plain-act/books/the-first-30-days-as-a-new-manager/

The feedback you avoid today usually becomes the performance problem you have to manage tomorrow.

New managers often delay difficult feedback because they want to be fair, avoid unnecessary tension, or wait for a ‘better moment.’

The delay rarely helps.

Small issues become patterns. Patterns become expectations. And by the time the conversation finally happens, the employee may reasonably wonder: ‘Why am I only hearing this now?’

Use a simple structure:

What happened → Why it matters → What needs to change next

What happened: Describe the specific behavior or result. No labels. No assumptions.

Why it matters: Explain the impact on the team, work, client, deadline, or standard.

What needs to change next: Set a clear expectation for the next time—and make sure both of you understand it.

Good feedback does not need to be harsh.

It needs to be timely, specific, and useful.

items.text:
New managers often think the first month is about proving they deserved the promotion. That pressure usually creates the opposite result: too much explaining, too many promises, delayed feedback, and work pulled back after delegation.

A steadier first month is simpler: observe before changing, make decisions clearly, give narrow feedback early, define the finish line when delegating, and protect enough capacity to actually manage.

The First 30 Days as a New Manager is a practical manual for that transition — authority, feedback, delegation, managing up, pushback, and decision timing without motivational hype.
